You buy a game before it's finished, provide bug reports and feedback to developers, and help shape a project's direction and ambitions. Everybody wins: You get to play the game early, and developers earn money that helps them continue and finish their work. It's been a boon for numerous notable games over the years, including Baldur's Gate 3 and Palworld .

In an interview with GamesRadar , though, Pocketpair communications and publishing chief John Buckley said that proposition is becoming increasingly difficult for developers, because the whole idea of early access has "lost its meaning."

"Go back to the Steam Greenlight days, when Steam changed Greenlight to early access, there were a few years where it really was running and operating exactly the way I think Steam dreamed it," Buckley said.

"I think everyone knew what they were in for. The kind of people who were buying early access games knew what they were in for. They were the kind of gamers who want to be involved, they want to give feedback, they want to talk to devs. It was this really beautiful golden era."

Now, though, the rise of what Buckley called "hyper-casual mobile culture, and hyper-casual gaming culture, and live service gaming culture" has eroded that understanding, and the accord between developer and gamer that rose from it: "The culture has changed and early access, essentially, has lost its meaning. People just buy an early access game like they buy a normal game and treat it like that's the game."

Path of Exile co-creator used to think 'live service was entirely upside, in all cases', but 10 years of experience and games like Baldur's Gate 3 have shown him another way GSC Game World says there's a reason it didn't give Stalker 2 more time in the oven: 'To make something better, you need to receive feedback, and this feedback should be fresh' Palworld studio says 'gamers don't want' AI in their games: 'It feels like everyone who is super gung-ho about it isn't from the industry' There's no doubt some truth to that. Generally speaking, I subscribe to the principle that if a product is offered for sale, and people pay money for that product, they're well within their rights to expect that they're getting the product. But early access isn't quite so cut-and-dried: Steam Greenlight was a more cumbersome system, but it also clearly delineated between a work-in-progress and a final release, which early access releases often do not.

Dialed-in gamers, or those who are old enough to remember when beta testing was an actual phase of development rather than a promotional tool, may have a clearer idea of what to expect from early access games. But as gaming becomes more of a mainstream pastime it's reasonable to expect that an increasing percentage of the audience is going to neither know nor care about what early access: They just want to buy a game and play it.

From the creators of Edge: A free weekly videogame industry newsletter, featuring in-depth news, expert analysis and exclusive interviews

Buckley doesn't believe that's necessarily a bad thing, but he did say "it's getting harder on Steam, sadly, because this culture has come through." And while he remains a believer, he also acknowledged that early access isn't ideal for every game, and that the system is "abused" by some developers.

"The biggest way it's abused now is just like, 'We'll release it now because we need money'," he said. "It's a way now to sidestep traditional funding means. It's almost become the new Kickstarter in some ways. Put out the build to get the money."

I'm not entirely sold on the idea that "put out the build to get the money" really qualifies as abuse—it is, after all, the whole basis for the early access system. But it can lead to trouble if early access sales aren't enough to support continued development, or simply through mismanaged expectations. The best thing developers who release into early access can do to avoid potential headaches, Buckley said, is to be clear about what's happening and, as much as possible, keep people fully informed.

"All we can do is try to softly educate people. I think we do an okay job. I think we try to be quite transparent. 'Hey guys, the next update's a while away. It's not going to be content-heavy, it's going to be QOL-heavy.' We try to balance it."

Players are spending money on a game that is unfinished, but at what point are they allowed to complain about the state the game they've bought is in if it has the early access label? According to Palworld communications and publishing lead John Buckley, back in the day players were a lot more aware of the state an early access game could be in, but now they're much more likely to expect a finished product.

"I think everyone knew what they were in for. The kind of people who were buying early access games knew what they were in for. They were the kind of gamers who want to be involved, they want to give feedback, they want to talk to devs. It was this really beautiful golden era," Buckley said in an interview with GamesRadar+ , describing the good old days when Steam Greenlight first shifted into Steam early access.

Today, that viewpoint doesn't really exist, mostly because of the integration of different gaming cultures on Steam. "This continuing migration, I'll call it, of hyper-casual mobile culture, and hyper-casual gaming culture, and live service gaming culture is washing through Steam right now. Now the culture has changed and early access, essentially, has lost its meaning. People just buy an early access game like they buy a normal game and treat it like that's the game."

The way that Buckley sees the situation right now, players will log on for a week or two, completely enthral themselves within a game, and then leave it thinking that there's not enough content coming quickly. "And you're like, 'Well guys, see you in six months. We've got to make the game.'"

Buckley doesn't want to throw shade at people who have this point of view, but he does think it's harder for developers on Steam thanks to this outlook. "All we can do is try to softly educate people. I think we do an okay job. I think we try to be quite transparent. 'Hey guys, the next update's a while away. It's not going to be content-heavy, it's going to be QOL-heavy.' We try to balance it," he said.

items.title: Palworld lead says Steam Early Access has “lost its meaning” as the "culture" has changed and players care less about how games are made
items.summary: Palworld publishing lead John Buckley believes that Steam Early Access has "lost its meaning" as players demand more content.
items.content:
Games Blog News Features FAQs Tutorials Palworld lead says Steam Early Access has “lost its meaning” as the “culture” has changed and players care less about how games are made Published:

Early access juggernaut Palworld is one of the biggest successes of the aforementioned early access phenomenon. While Palworld itself has seen success, publishing lead John Buckley says many are struggling due to how gamers treat the in-development service.

As many fans know, Steam Early Access was born out of the ill-fated Steam Greenlight program, and allowed developers to release unfinished titles that would grow with their audiences. This allows devs to fund development while working on the game, and has resulted in mega-hits like Valheim, Subnautica, and others.

In a discussion with GamesRadar , Bucket explained that Palworld developer PocketPair is “quite confident in early access in general”, but claims that gamers now treat it more like an ordinary game launch instead of the unfinished assisted development that it is designed to be.

“Go back to the Steam Greenlight days, when Steam changed Greenlight to early access, there were a few years where it really was running and operating exactly the way I think Steam dreamed it,” Buckley said.

“I think everyone knew what they were in for. The kind of people who were buying early access games knew what they were in for. They were the kind of gamers who want to be involved, they want to give feedback, they want to talk to devs. It was this really beautiful golden era.”

Buckley suggests that modern early access users are part of a “continuing migration” of “live-service gaming culture”. The Palworld lead argues that “early access, essentially, has lost its meaning… people just buy an early access game like they buy a normal game and treat it like that’s the game.”

One of the biggest issues with this new culture is the demand for new content, Buckley argues, as there’s a push for more while the game is still actively being made. He says that players will heavily play early access games for a period before saying: “‘These developers are not making new content. This game is dead.’ And you’re like, ‘Well guys, see you in six months. We’ve got to make the game.’”

Buckley does admit that early access isn’t perfect as a format for release, adding that “early access has not been abused for a lot of reasons”. Additionally, he admits that some gamers simply “aren’t interested” in development, but it does add more issues to the early access process.

“It’s getting harder on Steam, sadly, because this culture has come through. I think consoles are where it struggles the most because console gamers aren’t used to the concept of early access gameplay,” he said. “Again, that’s fine. You get less feedback from those players in general versus PC gamers, who love to drown you in bug reports. Look, all we can do is try to softly educate people. I think we do an okay job. I think we try to be quite transparent. ‘Hey guys, the next update’s a while away. It’s not going to be content-heavy, it’s going to be QOL-heavy.’ We try to balance it.”

Despite the issues, Buckley is still a fan of the early access formula, and PocketPair will continue to support it. “We’re big fans of it,” Buckley said.

Lewis White is a veteran games journalist with over a decade in the field. Starting with beloved Xbox website ICXM/XboxMAD, Lewis became the Gaming Editor at MSPoweruser before becoming the Editor in Chief of StealthOptional and Gfinityesports. Lewis later jumped to By Gamers For Gamers where he jumped to become EIC of VideoGamer and the host of the New VideoGamer Podcast prior to the website’s acquisition.

Over the years, Lewis has also seen long-form investigative pieces published in outlets such as Eurogamer, PCGamesN, Wireframe, Retro Gamer, Nintendo Life, and EDGE. Now, as the Editor in Chief of FRVR Blog, Lewis strives to bring the same level of quality journalism with interview-led content to the site in both written and audio form with the FRVR Podcast.

With a First Degree BA Hons in Games Journalism and Public Relations, Lewis has been a stable part of the British games press for over a decade, and has frequently displayed his love of Halo, The Elder Scrolls, Fallout, and other games pretty much everywhere he’s worked. And FRVR is no different.

Amidst Palworld's 1.0 early access graduation , Buckley discusses the work-in-progress approach with GamesRadar+. He maintains that Pocketpair is "quite confident in early access in general" and, when it comes time to make a new big thing, the studio will surely choose early access again. But that's despite what he sees as a big shift on Steam.

"Go back to the Steam Greenlight days, when Steam changed Greenlight to early access, there were a few years where it really was running and operating exactly the way I think Steam dreamed it," he says. "I think everyone knew what they were in for. The kind of people who were buying early access games knew what they were in for. They were the kind of gamers who want to be involved, they want to give feedback, they want to talk to devs. It was this really beautiful golden era."

Today, that outlook is less common, he suggests. "This continuing migration, I'll call it, of hyper-casual mobile culture, and hyper-casual gaming culture, and live service gaming culture is washing through Steam right now," Buckley notes. "Now the culture has changed and early access, essentially, has lost its meaning. People just buy an early access game like they buy a normal game and treat it like that's the game."

In Palworld's case, Buckley says players may buy the game in early access and play heavily for a week or two before arguing, "'These developers are not making new content. This game is dead.' And you're like, 'Well guys, see you in six months. We've got to make the game.'"

Buckley clarifies that he doesn't think "it's a bad thing that some gamers aren't interested" in how the sausage is made, even if quietly raising "the general knowledge level around game development" might help both sides. "You just want to enjoy a nice thing, and that's fair enough. No shade there." (In 2025, we spoke to dozens of game devs about things players get wrong about how games are made .)

Nonetheless, he says, "It's getting harder on Steam, sadly, because this culture has come through. I think consoles are where it struggles the most because console gamers aren't used to the concept of early access gameplay. Again, that's fine. You get less feedback from those players in general versus PC gamers, who love to drown you in bug reports. Look, all we can do is try to softly educate people. I think we do an okay job. I think we try to be quite transparent. 'Hey guys, the next update's a while away. It's not going to be content-heavy, it's going to be QOL-heavy.' We try to balance it."

Weekly digests, tales from the communities you love, and more

Recently, Buckley has been shaping expectations for update 1.1 , reiterating that Palworld will continue but is not due for another massive overhaul. Earlier in the year, he said he "wouldn't rule out a Palworld 2.0 ," but fans also shouldn't expect a No Man's Sky-style arrangement with 10 years of heavy support. (As it happens, we spoke to No Man's Sky boss Sean Murray about 10 years of support.)

Though Pocketpair has chosen early access multiple times and remain "big advocates" for it – Craftopia, its previous survival game, is approaching its own 1.0 update – Buckley agrees it's not right for every project.

"There are many real cases of early access just being a disaster for some games," he says. "I think it just depends on how receptive you want to be. Early access has now been abused for a lot of reasons. The biggest way it's abused now is just like, 'We'll release it now because we need money.' It's a way now to sidestep traditional funding means. It's almost become the new Kickstarter in some ways. Put out the build to get the money. But we're big fans of it."

Splashing some of its Palworld cash, Pocketpair's publishing arm has, like many other newly formed devs-turned-publishers, sought to find and fund promising games at a time of dire investment opportunities in the games industry.

items.title: Bushiroad announces 4.4 million pack sales for Palworld Official Card Game
items.summary: Bushiroad has announced over four million sales for Palworld’s card game.
items.content:
All News Bushiroad’s new Palworld card game is doing well (Image: Bushiroad/Pocketpair).

{" "} Bushiroad announces 4.4 million pack sales for Palworld Official Card Game .iframe-media {width: 100%;aspect-ratio: auto 16/9;} .img-media {width: 100%;aspect-ratio: auto 16/9;} .a-img-media {aspect-ratio: auto 16/9;} Bushiroad has announced over four million sales for Palworld’s card game. Bushiroad announced today (8 September) that the Palworld Official Card Game has officially hit over 4.4 million pack sales worldwide. The card game publisher noted in a news release that the Palworld Official Card Game’s booster pack Dawn of Palpagos had racked up millions of sales since launch.

Bushiroad had announced that the card game had hit 3.5 million pack sales earlier in July this year.

Palworld’s physical trading card game, Palworld Official Card Game, has released sales numbers via its publisher Bushiroad. According to the publisher, the card game’s booster pack Dawn of Palpagos has officially hit 4.4 million pack sales worldwide since its launch on 30 July, 2026.

The trading card game marked Pocketpair’s foray into the physical card game space along with veteran publisher Bushiroad, with the project first being announced in January this year. Palworld Official Card Game was then released simultaneously worldwide with its first booster pack, Dawn of Palpagos, which included over 50 Pals in newly-drawn illustrations, along with game characters like Zoe and Lily.

Dawn of Palpagos was also released alongside two trial decks, which were meant to help players start playing the card game immediately. The card game’s launch was evidently successful enough to have its demand spill over to eBay, where it was reported that some of its biggest chase cards were selling for four-figure sums in USD.

The Palworld Official Card Game is a two-player competitive card game that has players deploy teams of Pals, collect resources, deploy structures to control the field, and ultimately work towards victory. Each Pal comes with unique attributes to encourage different types of strategies during a match.

items.title: PlayStation Plus has dropped a bonus free offering for September 2026
items.summary: Following the September Essential tier reveal, a bonus offering has made its way to PlayStation Plus this month.
items.content:
Pokémon rival Palworld is attempting to lure in new players on PlayStation Plus.

Palworld , the popular Pokémon rival and open-world RPG, is free to try on PS5 right now for some PlayStation Plus subscribers. If you’ve been tempted to see what the hugely popular monster-collecting game is all about, there’s never been a better time to jump into Palworld and experience it for yourself.

Palworld , developed and published by indie studio Pocketpair, first launched in Early Access in January 2024 before officially leaving Early Access with its Version 1.0 update in July 2026.

Palworld is an open-world survival RPG that takes inspiration from Pokémon with its creature collecting, training and battling, while also incorporating crafting and survival mechanics reminiscent of games such as Minecraft . Unlike Pokémon, however, Palworld features robust online multiplayer, allowing players to team up with friends to explore, build and survive together, or turn against each other and become fierce rivals.

This week, a new PlayStation Plus Premium trial for Palworld launched , giving subscribers the perfect opportunity to try the popular survival RPG for free and decide whether it’s worth spending their hard-earned cash on.

PlayStation Plus Game Trials can vary significantly in length, with some lasting less than an hour and others offering up to five hours of gameplay. The Palworld trial sits somewhere in the middle, giving players a generous two hours to experience the full game.

During the two-hour Palworld trial, you’ll have full access to the game, can unlock trophies and, best of all, your save data will carry over to the full game if you decide to purchase it. There’s also an added incentive to take the plunge, as Palworld is currently 30% off on the PlayStation Store until September 9, 2026.

READ MORE: Pokémon rival Palworld unveils 'incredible' content update as it surpasses 40 million players

Palworld does have a story to follow, albeit a subtle one. A focus on the narrative takes a backseat, with its main emphasis being its open-world survival gameplay. Players can explore the Palpagos Islands, battle powerful bosses and uncover the mysteries surrounding the world and its Pals along the way.

In September 2024, Nintendo and The Pokémon Company sued Pocketpair, alleging that Palworld infringed several patents relating to gameplay mechanics. While the legal dispute remains ongoing, Pocketpair has since changed some of Palworld’s mechanics , including how Pals are summoned and how players can use them to glide through the world.

Claims of intellectual property infringement are always an interesting conversation, particularly in an industry where games have been building upon existing ideas for decades.

Pokémon itself has often been compared to Dragon Quest, with Dragon Quest V's monster-recruitment system frequently cited as an influence on Pokémon's creature-collecting concept. Meanwhile, Akira Toriyama's distinctive artwork for Dragon Quest has also been noted as an influence on the visual style of early Pokémon artwork.

Palworld is out now on PC, PlayStation and Xbox.

items.title: Pokemon-channeling Palworld courts fans through addictive play
items.summary: It would be fair to say that I’ve been out of the loop on AAA games the last few years. Big studios pushing wildly expensive product on a mostly cynical
items.content:
It would be fair to say that I’ve been out of the loop on AAA games the last few years. Big studios pushing wildly expensive product on a mostly cynical audience growing more cynical by the day did not exactly inspire confidence.

Especially when a single game costs somewhere in the ballpark of $70 (and developers think that’s too low — see speculation of GTA VI’s eventual price tag later this year). The last time I paid full price for a game was the Resident Evil 4 Remake, which took me back to pre-ordering the original for the Gamecube back in 2005.

Pokemon fans have long known that the price of a game does NOT go down over time. Nintendo fans in general accept this as something of an axiom. I played the original generation in 1998 quite a bit. Heck, I got an emulator, ROM and printed guide/walkthrough so that I could play and beat the second generation in Japanese before it came to North America.

Suffice it to say, I was a big Pokemon fan. I was out until, to quote Michael Corleone, they “pulled me back in” through a friend. That would’ve been the sixth generation around 2014 or so. I got a 3DS, Pokemon X and found myself reliving part of my childhood. I enjoyed the seventh generation, even if they occasionally seemed to run out of ideas, such as the introduction of a sandcastle Pokemon (they had earlier made an ice cream Pokemon, as well).

Then they moved from the 3DS to the Switch, which I don’t have. Pokemon had always been a handheld game, so the move seemed like an odd decision. That being said, The Pokemon Company empire knows what it is doing. Other AAA games take somewhere around $200 million or more to develop and can easily flop or merely break even. A Pokemon game costs around $10 to $20 million to develop and can generate around $1.5 billion in direct game sales.

It seemed they were indestructible, untouchable and what’s more is they knew it. Forget quality, just slap the name Pokemon on the product and it would sell like hotcakes. What could possibly go wrong?

Enter Palworld, “Pokemon with guns,” made by rival Japanese indie company Pocketpair as an open-world adventure game populated by “Pals,” which the player can battle or capture for combat, base building or traversal.

The early access version was released in January 2024 and reached a total number of players exceeding 25 million within one month. It peaked at more than 2 million concurrent players shortly after launch, something most AAA games never achieve.

Since the 1.0 full release July 10, it has roughly 400,000 concurrent players at any given moment on Steam. Critics (and Pokemon fans) point to the drop from the peak numbers, but those numbers for a game that released more than two years prior is nearly unheard of.

It’s also currently on Steam for $30, which for something of this magnitude and scope is quite the deal.

Jumping in, I initially had a feeling that Palworld’s core gameplay mechanics were similar to Minecraft, though I wouldn’t really know firsthand. You punch the tree to get wood, you punch the rock to get stone, then make a woodcutting axe and pickaxe with the materials you just gathered, improving your capabilities, build a home base and expand from there, rinse and repeat.

The slow grind and requirement that you (or your industrious Pals) craft everything yourself really gives weight to everything. You didn’t just find those cold-resistant clothes in a chest, you had to make them yourself. You can build a ranch, capture some of the sheep-like Pals and they will drop wool. Or you can go fight wild ones, who drop wool and lamb chops for cooking later.

I can’t be the only one who always thought about eating some of the cute little monsters in Pokemon. After all, who wouldn’t want to try some Magikarp sushi? In Palworld, your monster buddies need to eat, too. Morality aside, you can feed bacon to the pigs, if you get my drift.

To repeat myself, I do not own a Nintendo Switch or its aptly-named successor, The Switch 2, so I have not been able to play the newer Zelda games, but the climbing, hang gliding and stamina management seem copied directly, from what I know. You would think Nintendo would get litigious, which brings me to the next point.

items.title: This New Survival Game Finally Clicked with Me, and I'm Never Looking Back
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 does a great job of easing you into its many complex systems.
items.content:
Survival games have been wildly popular for years now. I’ve dabbled here and there to see what the fuss is about, but I’ve always fallen off after a few hours. Usually, I get tangled up in one meagerly explained system after another until I lose track of what I’m supposed to do, and my time with the game peters out.

When Palworld 1.0 came out to rave reviews , I figured I’d give the genre another shot – and I’m glad I did. Palworld’s gradual, newbie-friendly onboarding helped me see what a whole lot of people have loved about survival games all along. Palworld made me a believer.

I’m glad I came in at the 1.0 mark, because I’ve heard Palworld had a much steeper learning curve out of the gate. But now, new players start with a series of missions designed to guide you through the game’s numerous systems . You learn how to punch trees to get wood to create a crafting bench. You learn how to make a club you can use to beat some Pals to death (it’s a dog-eat-dog world out there) to get wool. You then use that wool to make clothes. You set up a camp. You build a house. You activate a teleporter and explore deeper into the game world.

Before long, you’re gliding off cliffs Zelda-style before whomping on every Pal you see to catch them in spheres to put them to work. You can deploy them at your camp, ride them , or have them fight by your side to take on big roaming Pals and towering bosses . It’s a blast. And there’s no way I would have stuck with it if it hadn’t held my hand and eased me into the systems that make up the game.

I still have a long way to go, because I was nowhere near powerful enough to defeat the first boss solo. But those early missions gave me a much-needed handle on what else I can spend my time doing as I level up enough to become a threat. There's a vast world out there I can keep exploring, all while catching Pals and building up my base. I’m having a blast doing it.

Palworld’s 1.0 is available on Steam , Xbox , and PS5 . It costs $29.99, but you can save a few bucks on a Steam copy at Fanatical , which is currently running its summer sale .

Chris Reed is a commerce editor and deals expert for IGN. He also runs IGN's board game and LEGO coverage. You can follow him on Bluesky .

items.title: Palworld 1.0 Review – Bigger, Better, and Still Brutally Addictive
items.summary: Palworld 1.0 is crammed with new content. More Pals, better quests, and a fully realized world for new and returning players to explore.
items.content:
Remember Palworld ? Well, the controversial game from Pocketpair finally has a 1.0 release. After two years, this feels like a very different animal than the one I initially encountered. The quest system is more complete, the UI is polished, and the world feels much more interconnected than before. While there are still some rough edges, this version of Palworld is a vastly improved one.

Now, I haven’t been keeping up with every iteration of Palworld released up to this point. So I’m not clear on how gradual or sudden these changes might be. But oh man, the quest system feels like night and day. You’re fed a steady stream of quests from the jump. They pair nicely with the tech tree, they appear on your map, and they sync with your compass. Yes, this is incredibly basic stuff. We figured out quest design decades ago. But you really appreciate the elegance of that design when it’s missing. Then when it finally shows up? It’s water in the desert.

Beyond the quests, it turns out Palworld works much better with connective tissue in place. Fast travel points, side quests, a detailed map, and distant objectives (like a floating island on the horizon) all make the world feel more tangible. Having an objective at all times kept me hooked on the game. Or at least, objectives are perfect for stringing you along until the factory sim element gets its claws in you. Once the big machine gets going, you don’t need anything else to maintain momentum.

The complete list of additions in Palworld 1.0 is downright intimidating. You can read the whole thing on their Steam page, but the highlights are remarkable. 72 new Pals, the Sunreach region, the World Tree, and an increased level cap all speak to a much larger, more complete game. There’s more of course, but the point remains – Palworld has undergone significant changes since the early access days.

This new version of Palworld still has some flaws, to be fair. The laptop I’m using is decently powerful, but I encountered a handful of framerate dips regardless. More important than the tiny performance issues is the core gameplay loop. Things hum along at a more relatable pace than ever before, sure. But you’re still faced with a pretty murderous grind. Pal levels creep upward slowly, and getting through that tech trees gets daunting quite quickly. While things start out breezy enough, the endgame is strictly for simulation psychopaths.

By which I mean the truly dedicated. Which is totally fine! There’s a fascinating disconnect between the monster battling and the base building. You can immerse yourself in one and ignore the other, at least for a hefty chunk of playtime. Although perhaps my impressions of the battling are skewed by hands off it all is. Your Pals run on autopilot, both in battle and beyond it. So for me, the fights are a diversion from my tiny empire.

In that regard, Palworld remains a specialized interest. Either you’re ready to get lost in the details of empire expansion and monster murder, or you’ll quickly lose momentum. The quest system, new content, and expanded Pal roster are all incidental in the face of this essential truth. The gooey caramel center that is the gameplay loop is more or less the same as it ever was. My mind was changed about this game, true. But I’m prone to hyper focus and bouts of mania. So a vast and ruthless machine like Palworld is straight up catnip for my badly wired brain.

The 1.0 release of Palworld presents a very different game than the original early access version. The quest system has been revamped, the map has been expanded, and civilization is scattered everywhere. But the gameplay loop is still pretty relentless. Plus, the rough edges haven’t been completely removed. If the old game was almost it for you, this new iteration might be exactly what you yearned for. But Palworld 1.0 is still an acquired taste.

***A Steam key was provided by the publisher***
